etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To scatter in different directions.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 15:7, column 1:
quote.text: The lippes of the wiſe diſperſe knowledge: but the heart of the fooliſh, doeth not ſo.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To break up and disappear; to dissipate.
(physics, transitive, intransitive) To separate rays of light, etc., according to wavelength; to refract.

quote.citation: 1998, James-Yves Roger, Technologies for the Information Society: Developments and Opportunities:
quote.text: Australia itself is a very wide and very disperse country, where the distance problems significantly affect also the "internal" customer-supplier chains.

quote.citation: 2014, Didier J. Dubois, Readings in Fuzzy Sets for Intelligent Systems, page 85:
quote.text: In particular, a very crisp quantifier such as “for all,” “there exists,” “at least 50 percent” tend to have less disperse weighting vectors while fuzzier quantifiers such as many tend to have a more disperse weighting vector.
